newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE - Flattening likely after Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE - Flattening likely after Greenspan.

text.p: After a week of doing absolutely nothing, analysts expect the U.S. Treasury yield curve to flatten in response to Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on Wednesday.
Odds favor a narrowing of spreads as Greenspan warns of inflation pressures, while suggesting short-term rates be held steady until evidence surfaces of higher consumer prices, players said.

"He's basically going to be telling the same story: inflation risks are out there ... but the Fed won't do anything until he sees inflation (actually) pick up," said Dominic Konstam, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
"The sense is that we are going to get a bullish flattening," he said.

Since last Wednesday, the spread between two-year notes and 30-year bonds has been locked in a range between 78 and 81 basis points, as the two-year note traded between 5.80 and 5.86 percent and the long bond between 6.58 and 6.66 percent.

Vincent Verterano, head trader at Nomura Securities International Inc, said that if Greenspan sticks to the same themes he has voiced over the past few months, the curve should not move all that much.
However, "If he gives a hint the Fed will tighten, it could flatten five basis points, but over two or three days, not immediately," Verterano added.
In the past, trying to predict what Greenspan might tell Congress has proved futile.

"He'll either be bullish or bearish," said John Williams, chief global economist at Bankers Trust Co. He noted that in recent months, it has been difficult to figure out the Fed, since Fed members talk of being pre-emptive on inflation, yet monetary policy has remained steady for a year.
Williams said the curve would steepen if Greenspan warned of inflation pressures but did not hint at a near-term tightening of monetary policy.
"To the degree people think the Fed is dragging its feet despite the fact the chairman sees inflation pressures building can't be good for the long end," he said.

That scenario is doubtful, said Williams, echoing the thoughts of most other players. Greenspan "will have to call a spade a spade," Williams said, "that things are working out well for the economy but that inflation risks are on the upside."

The key, though, is whether the market anticipates a tightening, analysts said. So, in the meantime, the long end looks to move -- responding to the inflation view -- as the short end ponders what the Fed will do.
"You can't really get bullish in the short end unless there's real evidence the economy is slowing down a lot," said Konstam. "You can't get away from the fact that the next (Fed) move is up."
